meeting_header: Date: 2026-01-27 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m | Attendees: Maya Chen, Jordan Reyes (Redwood) — Alex Moran, Priya Kapoor, Liam O'Hara (Ironcrest)
summary: Intro + qualification focused on security gating for hosted vs dedicated vs private. Customer requires SOC2/ISO evidence, BYOK KMS, SAML SSO, RBAC scoped to teams, 3 year audit log retention for certain endpoints, and low-latency in EU. Discussed fallback options and tradeoffs: hosted for speed, dedicated for predictable throughput, private for strict data residency. Agreed next steps: send docs and schedule technical deep dive.
topics: SSO / SAML and SSO flows (IdP integration)
RBAC and least-privilege for model access
Audit logging retention, log export and SIEM integration
Encryption at rest/in transit and BYOK/HSM options
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (latency, cost, data residency)
transcript: [00:00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone thanks for joining — quick intro from our side, I'm Maya (AE) and Jordan is our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Alex (Ironcrest): Hi, Alex here. Good, thanks. We wanted to surface our security gating up front — so appreciate the time.

[00:00:20] Priya (Ironcrest): Priya here — head of infosec. Main asks: SOC2 or ISO evidence, SSO with our Okta, BYOK for keys, and audit logs retention — some of our regs require up to three years for certain telemetry.

[00:00:35] Jordan (Redwood): Great, thanks Priya. We can walk through how Redwood supports each. Quick note — sometimes our docs refer to "Redwood Dedicated" and "Private" differently, I'll try to call them consistently.
[00:00:48] Alex: Perfect. One quick question: when you say BYOK, do you mean customer-managed keys in the cloud KMS or physically separated HSM?

[00:01:00] Jordan: We support both patterns. For hosted deployments we offer CMEK via customer cloud KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS/Azure KeyVault). For Private we can integrate with on-prem HSM or bring-your-own HSM for FIPS-level needs. There's an option for HSM-backed KMS for Dedicated if you have an enterprise contract — it's a controlled flow.
[00:01:20] Priya: So for cloud hosting we retain keys with KMS but you still hold the key material? We need to ensure we have rotation and explicit audit trails when keys are used.

[00:01:34] Jordan: Correct. With CMEK logs show key usage; key rotation policies are customer controlled. We also emit KMS usage events into audit logs which you can forward to your SIEM via S3/BigQuery export or direct connector.

[00:01:48] Priya: Good. About audit log retention — we have a compliance requirement: service-level logs for model access and data exfil events retained for at least 36 months. Is that supported with hosted?

[00:02:02] Maya: Hosted can retain logs but long-term retention is typically an add-on — we can configure extended retention and offload to customer storage. For strict residency and retention SLAs many customers choose Dedicated or Private so they own the storage lifecycle.
[00:02:18] Alex: So with Hosted you'd rely on Redwood to store logs unless we configure export? We prefer we control the retention windows and encryption at rest for those archives.

[00:02:29] Jordan: Yes — we have automatic export hooks. A typical pattern: short-term logs kept in Redwood for quick troubleshooting, and then an automated export to your S3 bucket with lifecycle policies you control for long-term retention and encryption. That meets the need for customer-controlled retention and encryption in transit.
[00:02:45] Priya: Ok. Next: SSO. We run Okta, SAML 2.0. Can we enforce SCIM provisioning and org-scoped RBAC so only certain teams can call specific models?

[00:02:58] Maya: Absolutely — we support SAML SSO and SCIM for user provisioning. Our console supports RBAC roles (admin, developer, viewer) and can scope API keys by project/route level. Jordan, do you want to add detail?

[00:03:08] Jordan: Sure. We provide token-level scoping so you can create service tokens that are limited to embeddings or generation or to a model family. RBAC integrates with SSO directory groups, so you can map Okta groups to Redwood roles programmatically.
[00:03:24] Liam (Ironcrest): When you say token-level scoping, will those tokens still be usable from external clients, or can we enforce network egress rules?

[00:03:33] Jordan: Good callout. Dedicated and Private can be configured in a VPC with private endpoints and allow-listing of client IPs or VPC peering. Hosted endpoints are public but can be restricted via network allow-lists and API gateway usage. If you need zero public egress, Private (on-prem/VPC with no internet egress) is the pattern.
[00:03:50] Alex: We also care about data residency — EU-only. Do you have EU-hosted regions and data plane separation?

[00:03:57] Maya: Yes, we have regionalized data planes. For EU residency customers typically use either Hosted in EU region or Dedicated pools provisioned in EU. Private is for full on-prem or customer VPC with control over where data lives.
[00:04:10] Priya: Encryption in transit — TLS is fine but we also need proof of mutal TLS for service-to-service in the Private setup. Is that supported?

[00:04:20] Jordan: mTLS is supported for Private and can be configured for Dedicated in certain hosting patterns. For Hosted we use strong TLS; we can integrate client cert auth for certain enterprise customers.
[00:04:34] Priya: About audit logs content — we need model input hashes (not raw inputs) in logs for privacy — do you have options to redact or hash inputs before logging?

[00:04:46] Jordan: We do. There's a configurable logging policy: full logging, redacted, or schema-based structured logs where we only emit metadata and hashes. For regulated workloads many customers choose to never persist raw inputs — we can do per-route logging policies.
[00:05:02] Alex: What about KV cache or prefix caching — could that be exposing sensitive tokens?

[00:05:09] Jordan: The runtime's KV cache is ephemeral and encrypted in memory. For longer-term caches we recommend customer-managed encrypted stores. Also you can opt out of prefix caching for sensitive routes.
[00:05:19] Maya: A note on terminology — sometimes the transcription says K-V cash, but it's KV cache.
[00:05:25] Priya: Ha, noted. On model rollouts: we need ability to pin model versions and have rollbacks with audit trails who triggered them.
[00:05:33] Jordan: Rollouts are auditable; all admin actions are recorded with actor identity from SSO. You can require 2-person approval for production rollouts via RBAC workflows.
[00:05:44] Liam: For latency — our worst-case target is 100ms p50 for short prompts for EU region. Hosted is faster to onboard but is it realistic?

[00:05:53] Jordan: Depends on model family and token lengths. Hosted can meet low-latency for certain optimized models and with prefix caching. Dedicated gives predictable p50/p95 and you can reserve GPU shapes to hit your SLA. Private avoids cross-region hops but means you manage infra.
[00:06:08] Alex: If we run a pilot, can we test both Hosted in EU and a Dedicated pool to compare tail latency and cost?
[00:06:15] Maya: Yes — typical pilot includes a week of comparison with synthetic load and a short canonical prompt set. Jordan will set up the benchmark harness.
[00:06:22] Jordan: I'll prepare a benchmark template — would like your sample traffic and peak qps, Liam. Also will need sample prompts so we pick a representative model size.
[00:06:33] Priya: About pen testing and compliance — do you allow external audits and pen tests against the Dedicated or Private deployments?
[00:06:42] Jordan: For Dedicated and Private, customers can do pen testing with agreed scope. Hosted has a controlled pen test program; we share reports (redacted) and have third-party attestations.
[00:06:54] Alex: Ok. One of our legal asks: indemnities around data leakage — we need to review your contract with redlines. Should we send our standard security addendum?
[00:07:03] Maya: Yes, please send it to us. I'll involve our legal/ops team. We'll also attach standard security addendum and SOC2 artifact set in return.
[00:07:12] Priya: For key rotation, do you offer automated key rotation or is that for customers to manage in their KMS?

[00:07:20] Jordan: If you're using CMEK, rotation is customer controlled via your KMS. We can integrate rotation hooks so the service picks up new keys without downtime. For managed keys we rotate per our policies and publish rotation logs.
[00:07:34] Alex: Any notable limitations? For example, can we host private models with restricted internet egress?

[00:07:40] Jordan: Private can be fully air-gapped if needed — but that requires an on-prem deployment package and support contract. Dedicated in customer VPC can also be configured to block egress — we just need to design networking.
[00:07:51] Priya: Can you forward audit logs into our Splunk instance?
[00:07:55] Jordan: Yes, we have forwarders and native integrations for Splunk, Datadog, S3, BigQuery — we can push events or provide a pull endpoint.
[00:08:05] Liam: What about PBIs — per-route quotas and throttling for production? We want per-team rate limiting with alerting.
[00:08:12] Jordan: Rate limits and quotas are configurable by project and token. Alerts can be sent to PagerDuty or Slack via webhooks.
[00:08:20] Alex: Great. We're also considering Megawatt AI — they claim HSM-backed encryption by default. How do you compare?

[00:08:27] Maya: Megawatt has HSM-first positioning; we offer optional HSM for enterprise and stronger controls via Private. Many customers choose Redwood for the unified runtime and transparent cost controls plus flexibility to move between Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
[00:08:40] Priya: Cost question: long-term retention of logs for 3 years — is there a rough estimate of costs?
[00:08:46] Maya: We'll provide a BOQ — generally long-term S3-based retention is the most cost efficient and we'll itemize it in the pilot pricing.
[00:08:56] Jordan: I'll include a sample cost model showing host cost + export storage + dedicated reservation vs hosted over a 12 month horizon.
[00:09:05] Alex: Ok let's recap next steps before we close.

[00:09:08] Maya: Recap: Redwood to share SOC2, ISO summaries and security whitepaper; SE to schedule deep-dive and benchmark; Ironcrest to provide traffic profile, retention specifics, and security addendum. Agreed to aim for tech deep-dive week of Feb 2nd.
[00:09:24] Priya: That works. Also will circulate our list of regulated data classes and a contact for legal redlines.
[00:09:30] Maya: Great. Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the docs.
[00:09:35] Alex: Thanks, bye.
[00:09:36] Meeting ended
